title: Relic and Gumi: Governing Memory, Safety, and Continuity in Diegetic Relational Agents
comment: 51 pages, 3 figures; exploratory two-participant Telegram pilot; HCI systems paper
summary:
Longitudinal relational agents rely on memory for continuity, but remembering can lead to intrusion, clinical overconfidence, emotional manipulation, and opacity. We present Relic, a governance architecture for diegetic relational agents, and Gumi, a subject-specific companion agent initialized and governed through Relic. The architecture separates what the system can observe, what researchers can review, what Gumi can remember, and what Gumi can say.
  We describe three mechanisms. Relic represents sensitive safety signals as researcher-facing governance objects rather than user-facing explanations or agent memories. Shared Continuity Memory organizes relational markers around subject-confirmed wording, corrections, explicit follow-up permissions, and recall limits. We specify a runtime mediation layer for delivery, proactivity, session identity, output transformation, and platform allowlists; adoption across live paths remains partial. These mechanisms aim to preserve relational continuity without turning Gumi into a clinical assistant, mood tracker, general-purpose assistant, or opaque profiling system.
  We contribute the architecture, object model, researcher workbench design, and a proposed evaluation framework for governed relational memory. An exploratory pilot involved the author as P1 and one external participant as P2. Weekly self-reports from P1 and researcher-led interviews with P2 provide descriptive observations of early use and perceived naturalness. The pilot does not support claims about clinical efficacy, diagnosis, therapeutic outcomes, general usability, or deployment safety. Relic provides research infrastructure intended to make relational memory, safety constraints, and agent behavior inspectable and testable.

title: Seeing Is Not Knowing: The Epistemic Limits of LLM-Based Mental Health Inference from Youth Social Media Conversations
summary: Adolescents increasingly use social media for private conversations, sharing experiences and seeking support. These interactions generate digital traces, prompting efforts to infer mental health and psychosocial states. As large language models become more capable of reasoning about conversations and interpersonal dynamics, a fundamental question remains nonetheless: what can models actually "know" about an individual's psychological experience from what they are able to "see"? We evaluated ten reasoning LLMs using donated Instagram Direct Messages from 80 adolescents with a history of depression or suicidal thoughts and behaviors, comparing predictions with self-reports and analyzing 204 reasoning traces. Models performed better when inferring more observable states than participants' subjective appraisals of social experience, such as perceived social support. Beyond prediction accuracy, our findings highlight the epistemic limits of digital traces for AI design and evaluation: what can be observed, what can reasonably be inferred, and what requires people's own accounts.

title: Goals as a Representational Layer for Human-AI Collaboration
summary: Goals are central to how people, teams, and organizations structure their work. Yet, while generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly operate across a worker's context, information about why a person is pursuing a task, beyond local prompts and interactions, is typically missing. We argue that goals should become an explicit representational layer mediating interactions among people, AI systems, and organizations. Because human goals are hierarchical, partially latent, and dynamically evolving, such a layer must be multidimensional, both grounded in human articulation and inferred from available evidence, and continuously updated. A goal layer could connect immediate requests to broader outcomes, improve the organization and retrieval of relevant context, support reflection and coordination, and provide a foundation for training, aligning, and evaluating AI systems in terms of human-centered outcomes. We highlight these opportunities while identifying open challenges involving goal inference, socio-cognitive frictions, alignment, privacy, and governance.

title: Learning from How Users Interpret: Personalizing Recommendation Explanation Order
summary: Personalized explanations typically adapt their content or presentation based on preferences, interaction histories, or other user characteristics. We examine whether regularities inferred from prior textual interpretations can support personalization of explanation organization. In a controlled within participant study with 122 participants, prior interpretations were represented along three dimensions: information selection, relative salience, and relational organization. The relational dimension was partially operationalized through co mobilization. These representations were aggregated into fixed historical profiles and used to organize otherwise identical explanation sentences. Participants encountered four organization procedures: the OWN historical profile, the DONOR historical profile, a population profile called POP, and a language model procedure using the historical profile called PROFILE LLM. Post exposure objective comprehension was the primary outcome. OWN achieved 86.5 percent correct responses, compared with 66.0 percent for DONOR, 63.9 percent for POP, and 73.0 percent for PROFILE LLM. Mixed effects analyses showed higher comprehension with OWN than with each alternative procedure. No reliable overall condition effect was detected for recommendation acceptance. These findings indicate that historical profiles derived from prior interpretations can provide an actionable signal for personalizing explanation order while keeping explanatory content and wording fixed.

title: MotionDecipher: LLM-Assisted Clinical Interpretation of Human Motion Signals for Efficient Gait Analysis
comment: 33 pages, 19 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies (IMWUT), Vol. 10, No. 4, Article 245, December 2026
summary: Clinical gait and motion analysis is widely used to guide targeted interventions for patients with neurological disorders, the outcome of which is typically a report with descriptions of joint movements and forces. Current practices rely on experts' manual effort, which is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide opportunities to address this problem, but translating human motion into clinical gait descriptions remains challenging because the quality of the context directly affects LLMs' reasoning capability over continuous motion signals. To tackle this, we introduce MotionDecipher, a novel framework bridging the semantic gap between motion data and clinical interpretations. Specifically, we made 3 key advancements: 1) a Human Motion Tokenizer that converts motion signals into domain-specific tokens for time- and frequency-informed gait interpretation; 2) a Meta Feature Selector that transforms tokens into Structured Representations; and 3) a Hybrid Context Constructor to determine the optimal demonstration-based prompt for In-Context Learning. We evaluated MotionDecipher on data collected at an accredited gait lab from 122 patients and 46 controls. Results show that MotionDecipher achieves 0.91 BERTScore (13% over GPT-5), while expert evaluation ranks MotionDecipher highest in Correctness, Completeness, and Conciseness compared to baselines, highlighting its promise for efficient gait analysis.

title: Driver Takeovers and Longitudinal Responses Analysis from Naturalistic Driving
comment: 28 pages, 14 figures. See arXiv:2603.06986 for the companion dataset paper. The longitudinal subset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HenryYHW/ADAS-TO_longitudinal
summary: As Level 2 advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) become more widely used, understanding driver-system interaction is increasingly important for traffic safety. However, limited real-world data make these interactions difficult to study. We present ADAS-TO, a naturalistic dataset of 16,446 takeover clips from 364 drivers across 2,585 different drives. It combines road video, vehicle kinematics, driver inputs, and ADAS status. To analyze takeover behavior, we retained 6,206 manually reviewed takeover events during continued lane keeping or car following. We excluded events in which the driver intentionally changed lanes, turned, or made a stop beyond the ADAS's capabilities (e.g., at a red light or stop sign) shortly after takeover. Drivers began intervening before ADAS disengaged in 65.6% of takeovers involving braking or steering. When the ego vehicle was still closing on a lead vehicle at disengagement, longitudinal safety margins often narrowed further after the transfer to manual control. Among 2,031 such events, 78.5% had a lower minimum time-to-collision (TTC) in the five seconds after disengagement than in the five seconds before it. For events involving braking, the mean TTC trajectory reached its minimum about 1.2 s after disengagement. We model the subsequent braking response using a Gazis-Herman-Rothery (GHR) car-following law. Its median five-second spacing root-mean-square error is 1.34 m with observed lead motion and 1.84 m with predicted lead motion. The fitted model expresses braking as a response to looming, with stronger responses at higher speeds and shorter gaps. Applied before takeover, it shows that greater looming than predicted by the human-response reference is associated with disengagement. These findings support continued assessment of longitudinal safety after ADAS disengagement, while the driver's braking response develops.

title: Lea: An Agent Backbone for Mathematician-Controlled Formalization in Lean
summary: Agentic systems now formalize research-level mathematics in Lean, but they are built for autonomy: the mathematician states a target and inspects a result. The alternative, a general-purpose coding harness, is domain-neutral and must be assembled into a formalization workspace before any mathematics begins. Mathematicians, however, report wanting to keep high-level control over how an argument is decomposed and established. We present $\textbf{Lea}$, a Lean-specific agent backbone for mathematician-facing software rather than a single interface. Lea exposes runs, sessions, and typed events through one application-neutral API, and ships with Lean tooling (blueprints, LSP, Loogle, SafeVerify) already wired. We report two applications built on it: $\textbf{LeaChat}$, a web client for interactive proof authoring, and $\textbf{LeaOverleaf}$, which formalizes theorems annotated directly in an Overleaf document; a session begun in either continues in the other. In a case study, a mathematician outlined a proof of the Durfee square generating function in a few natural-language messages, and Lea produced a complete Lean development from Mathlib alone, following the intended decomposition closely and requiring substantive correction at a single point. Lea and both applications are released as open source so that further mathematician-facing tools can be built on the same backbone.

title: "I had nobody to turn to": Why LGBTQ+ People Choose (Not) to Use AI Chatbots for Personal Health and Relationship Advice
summary: While there is an abundance of research into large language model (LLM) biases against LGBTQ+ communities, far less research has examined how and why LGBTQ+ people choose to make use of AI chatbots. In this work, we examine how LGBTQ+ people choose (not) to use AI chatbots across three domains in which LGBTQ+ users have unique needs: relationship support, mental health support, and gender or sexual health support. We surveyed 73 people (60 LGBTQ+; 13 non-LGBTQ+) on how they interact with AI chatbots and find that participants' access to external resources, privacy concerns, and perceptions of chatbot capabilities shape whether and how they choose to make use of AI chatbots. For instance, some LGBTQ+ participants felt that chatbots might actually be less biased against LGBTQ+ people than the people they know offline. We also find that LGBTQ+ participants report using AI chatbots less frequently than non-LGBTQ+ participants across 15 specific personal health and relationship advice scenarios, citing concerns about AI sycophancy and adverse cognitive side-effects. Recognizing AI chatbots as vital (albeit imperfect) resources for LGBTQ+ people, we recommend researchers consider systemic issues that drive users to AI chatbots and design technologies (AI or otherwise) that prioritize privacy, anonymity, and real human connection.

title: Bidirectional Modeling of mmWave Human Signals for Enhancement & Synthesis
summary: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) is attractive for human-centered robotics in smoke, darkness, and privacy-sensitive indoor spaces: it measures reflections rather than visually identifiable imagery and remains usable without light. Deployed systems, however, face two complementary needs that run in opposite directions. Enhancement starts from a raw range-angle-Doppler (RAD) heatmap, where human returns coexist with nonhuman structure, and aims to isolate the human signal by removing nonhuman returns, yielding a clean RAD input for downstream perception. Synthesis starts from denser human geometry and aims to synthesize natural RAD observations, including environmental and hardware features, thereby expanding scarce supervision data. Although the two tasks reverse direction, both require modeling how human and nonhuman reflections coexist in the same measurement. Among RAD axes, Doppler provides motion information native to the modality, with the potential to support this modeling. We therefore cast both tasks on the dual-domain RAD heatmap and propose HeatWave, which injects Doppler when it is locally reliable, and routes Doppler asymmetrically for enhancement and synthesis within one shared backbone. This design improves both tasks: enhanced observations reduce mean per-joint position error by 11.4% relative to the raw recording, and synthesized samples that replace half of the real radar labels recover most of the activity accuracy lost to the reduced budget. Relative to an unspecialized dual-task heatmap baseline, the enhancement improves motion-critical samples under metallic clutter by 2.3times more than when geometry already suffices, and synthesis follows the same ordering with a narrower spread, providing the community with a research direction more closely aligned with the signal's characteristics.

title: The Relational Capacity Framework: A Lens for AI-Mediated Relationality
summary: A growing literature examines the impact of engaging with AI chatbots on our relationality: our ability to form relationships with others, maintain them through life's changes, and exit when needed. Currently, substantial work focuses on purpose-built AI companions (e.g. Replika, Character.AI), with less work investigating socioemotional uses of the more widely-used general-purpose chatbots. In this paper, we present a 100-person investigation into how people engage general-purpose AI for socioemotional needs. Participants' AI uses varied, from practicing specific social skills to seeking additional bandwidth and information as they navigated their social contexts. To explain this heterogeneity, we provide 8 states that describe how AI expands or contracts relationality for people with different levels of skills, bandwidth, and information. We then present a unified conceptual model for the role of technology in mediating human relationality, the Relational Capacity Framework, and outline future research designing appropriate roles for AI in human connection.

title: The Drawing You Watch Is the Portrait You Keep: A Replayable Machine Portrait Studio
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. Live system: https://everyfaceproject.com
summary: Ask an image model for your portrait and a finished picture arrives: no first line, no second thoughts, no record of how it got there, and a different picture if you ask again. I built a portrait studio that works the other way. A sitter chooses one of eight fictional artists, each written with a city, a medium and a tempo of its own, holds still for 8 to 12 seconds, and watches a drawing of themselves appear over 44 seconds. One still is sent after consent, a hosted image model returns a private study the sitter never sees, and a compiler turns that study into one drawing document. The live drawing, the saved sheet, the vector export and the film all read that document, and a replay makes no model call, so the drawing you watch is the portrait you keep. I describe the compiler in enough detail to rebuild it and say plainly what it is: an authored reconstruction at a compressed speed, not a recorded hand. On 16 generated test studies a sheet holds 8,784 to 16,378 timed contacts, about three quarters of them fixed-grid fills and nearly all shorter than one video frame, and recompiling one study gave byte-identical output four times on one machine. The paper also traces a bug that matters more than any of that. The earlier compiler estimated the paper colour tile by tile, read dark skin as paper, and in all eight hands kept less of a deep-complexioned face than a fair one (13 to 48 percent against 41 to 56). On 80 generated studies the rebuilt engine keeps the complexion difference the study already has (raw retention 89 to 120 percent), so the fairness question has moved upstream, to the study and the hosted model. The two test sitters are generated and differ in more than complexion, and no real-face or perceptual study exists yet. The studio is live at https://everyfaceproject.com.

title: "Despite her age, Margaret was eager to make a change": Unpacking Aging Representations and Stereotypes in LLM-generated Stories
summary: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate everyday stories, their portrayals can shape expectations about aging. Prior work has largely examined age stereotypes in short responses, leaving unanswered whose lives models default to imagining and how age shapes characters' roles in complete narratives. We analyze 594 stories generated by Gemini, GPT, and Llama using text embeddings, LLM-assisted coding, and qualitative analysis. When age was unspecified, stories typically featured younger adults, with middle-aged protagonists largely absent. Older adults were often portrayed through loss, familiar routines, and help from younger characters. Even positive stories sometimes treated older adults' achievements as surprising or portrayed others making decisions on their behalf. We suggest evaluating not only the tone of generated stories, but also who appears, what opportunities they receive, and who makes decisions. Involving older adults in these evaluations can guide writing tools toward more varied, less stereotyped portrayals of later life.

title: Rhythmic Fitness Beat 'Em All using Real-Time Monocular Human Pose Estimation
summary: Short and frequent physical activity exercices mitigate the health risks of sedentary behavior. Yet, the lack of motivation remains a critical barrier to adoption. Exergames gamify physical activity, but most rely on dedicated hardware, and outside dance and rhythm games they rarely use the musical beat. We present a work-in-progress beat 'em up exergame played with the whole body in front of a single smartphone, which runs the entire pipeline: an off-the-shelf real-time 3D human mesh recovery model on the phone's neural processing unit, gesture recognition, and the game, shown on any TV through a USB-C to HDMI cable. Our contributions are (1) a 3D recognition of five shadow-boxing moves (guard, punch, slip, squat, jump), each defined by one metric measure in a body frame aligned with gravity and one threshold with hysteresis, personalised during a tutorial; (2) a rhythm stage whose discrete cues are placed on the song's kick drum and judged on the movement's capture time, with a delay learned for each player; and (3) a phone-only architecture, running at 30 frames per second, that turns a phone and an HDMI cable into an exergame console.

title: Thinking Twice: A Sequential Approach to Nudge Towards Reflective Judgment in GenAI-Assisted Decision Making
comment: Full paper accepted and presented at the 20th International Conference on Wirtschaftsinformatik (WI 2025), Münster, Germany. To appear in the conference proceedings (Lecture Notes in Information Systems and Organisation, Springer). This version is the submitted manuscript prior to peer review
summary: Humans increasingly use generative AI (GenAI) for decision-making assistance, yet tend to engage in such situations using quick, intuitive (System 1) rather than deliberate, analytical assessment (System 2) as reflected in Dual Process Theory. Such engagement reduces the effectiveness of human-GenAI interactions and increases associated risks. Our research investigates how to design human-GenAI interactions that promote the transition from System 1 to System 2 thinking in decision-making. Based on the Three-Stage-Model, which suggests humans switch to System 2 when conflicts are detected, we conducted an experiment (n=130) testing sequential human-GenAI interaction as a cognitive forcing nudge during problem-solving tasks. This approach, where humans decide first before receiving AI assistance, enables detection of conflicting decisions. Compared to non-sequential settings (concurrent or no AI assistance), results show the sequential condition significantly enhanced both decision performance and GenAI prompt utilization, providing valuable insights for designing more reflective and thus effective human-GenAI interactions.

title: Sensed but Not Told: Hidden Physiological Adaptation Shapes LLM Persuasion
summary: Wearable sensors, including those embedded in VR headsets, can provide LLM-based chatbots with physiological signals that users do not explicitly communicate. We tested whether such hidden input changes persuasion. In a $2\times2$ within-subjects study ($N=24$), a chatbot argued against participants' self-selected opinions with or without turn-level heart-rate and pupil-diameter features; sensing was disclosed halfway through the study. Before disclosure, sensing increased perceived persuasiveness by 1.42 points. Across the study, sensing was associated with a 0.57-point greater shift toward the chatbot's position and 3.20 times the odds of any movement toward it. Persuasiveness ratings were lower after disclosure, although disclosure was confounded with session order. Dialogue logs suggested a more declarative interaction style when sensing was on: chatbot replies contained question marks less often, and conversations contained fewer turns. These findings motivate making biosignal-driven adaptation inspectable and providing a genuinely non-sensed mode.

title: DeepRadio: A Human-Agent Workspace for Physical Radio Development
summary: Agentic programming can automate software-defined radio (SDR) development, but decisions can propagate from software to hardware without sufficient user visibility or control. We present DeepRadio, a human-agent workspace embedded in GNU Radio Companion (GRC) for jointly constructing, verifying, and operating physical radio systems. DeepRadio uses a dynamic and state-driven workflow to coordinate a traceable radio specification, claim-oriented cross-layer verification, and mixed-initiative control. These mechanisms expose decisions, tie conclusions to available evidence, and return control to users before consequential hardware actions. Across seven atomic SDR tasks, DeepRadio completed nearly all runs while satisfying all prescribed software and radio-frequency constraints. In a 20-participant study, more participants achieved a verified physical deployment with DeepRadio than with Codex-assisted GRC. Participants reported stronger support for shared intent and understanding while retaining initiative and control. These results suggest that DeepRadio can make agent-assisted physical radio development more reliable, understandable, and controllable.

title: Entering a New Domain in the Era of Generative AI: An Autoethnography of Solo Game Development as a Bioinformatics Educator
summary: The rapid improvement of generative AI (GenAI) not only increased the efficiency of practice but also empowered individuals with capabilities to explore new domains. However, identity formation in the wake of such empowerment remains understudied. We use an autoethnography to understand identity formation in the context of solo game development as a bioinformatics educator. With the goal of developing a create-your-own-adventure (CYOA) game, we collected data for 73 days through journal entries, interacting with communities of practices. The autoethnographer had continuously reassessed the situation, and closely interacted with communities of practice. Their prior knowledge was used to provide in-game context and to uniquely interpret game development processes. These findings suggest that the autoethnographer made efforts to belong to communities of practice and engaged extensively in sensemaking through the lens of a bioinformatics educator. Although GenAI puts power at hand, attaining a new identity took place at a human pace.

title: GroundWork: Bridging Human and LLM Reasoning Through a Structured Argumentation Model
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into workflows that require reasoning over text documents, yet interaction remains largely conversational. This leaves argumentative structure implicit or embedded in text, making it difficult to maintain, compare, and revise arguments as analyses evolve. We present GroundWork, a mixed-initiative system that makes argument structure a shared, editable state for humans and LLMs. GroundWork operationalizes the Toulmin model of argumentation as a typed graph with explicit operations for human and LLM edits. It exposes this structure through coordinated corpus views and an editable workbench for constructing, comparing, testing, and tracing source-grounded arguments. We evaluate GroundWork through an expert study with four participants spanning consulting, product development, law, and immunology, and three use-case scenarios in intelligence, law, and medicine. Our findings show that GroundWork makes source-grounded arguments inspectable, comparable, and revisable as shared human-LLM state.
